amstar2_items.justification: Research questions and eligibility criteria are framed around realist Context-Mechanism-Outcome (CMO) configurations (population: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples; geography: Australia; phenomenon: Indigenous engagement in mandatory-compliance government drinking water policy linked to accountability mechanisms) rather than PICO intervention/comparator/outcome elements.

No a priori registered or published protocol for this drinking water realist review (e.g., PROSPERO or OSF) is reported, and no protocol deviations are addressed (Fono et al. 2024 is cited only regarding the Co-design Brains Trust governance structure, not as a protocol for this review).

Sections 2.5–2.7 explain the selection of a realist review design capable of integrating diverse evidence types (qualitative and quantitative studies alongside downloadable government policy documents, reports, and local case studies) to build a CMO programme theory.

Authors searched 8 databases/engines in May 2024 (PubMed, Medline, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Academic Search Premier, AIATSIS, Google Scholar) with assistance from a university librarian, reported full Boolean search strings, and searched grey literature portals and government websites; however, they did not report searching reference lists of included studies or trial/study registries, nor justify English-language restriction beyond translation convenience.
Authors 1–3 screened titles/abstracts and reviewed full texts against eligibility criteria, with Author 2 resolving discrepancies.

Data extraction was performed by a single reviewer (Author 1) and subsequently verified by co-authors (Authors 2–6 and 9), rather than independent duplicate extraction or >=80% consensus calibration on a sample.
Although a PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1) is referenced, no bibliographic list of excluded full-text articles with individual study-level reasons for exclusion is provided in the text or appendices.

Table 1 reports only Evidence type, Author/year, Title, and System level (Macro/Meso/Micro); it omits study designs, methods, sample sizes/populations, specific policy mechanisms, and study-level findings despite Section 2.9 stating these were extracted.

In Appendix A, the 5 'peer-reviewed' items (themselves secondary reviews, a policy/legal commentary, an industry report, and a perspective paper) were appraised using a custom cultural-relevance checklist plus JBI Systematic Review or JBI Textual Evidence: Expert Opinion checklists rather than primary-study risk-of-bias tools, and the 33 grey literature documents/case studies/media items received no formal risk-of-bias assessment.
Sources of funding for the individual included studies and reports are not reported.
No quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis was conducted; synthesis used thematic coding into realist CMO configurations and collaborative yarning circles.

Although Section 5 notes generally that the rigour of local case studies may be subject to scrutiny and Section 4 notes the dominance of non-Indigenous-led research, the synthesis does not account for the low appraisal scores and flagged bias concerns in Appendix A (e.g., Study 1 ~35% and Study 2 ~54% flagged with 'questionable sources, political bias concern', Study 3 ~41%) when relying on those sources for core claims.
Qualitatively explains substantial heterogeneity across macro (national), meso (state/territory), and micro (local/remote vs. urban) jurisdictions and governance arrangements across Australia.

Funding sources (Macquarie University, UNSW, Australian Government RTP Scholarship, Onehealth Organisation), a no-conflict-of-interest declaration, and a detailed author positionality statement are transparently reported (though note co-author B. Moggridge authored several included items).

raw_response.methodological_notes: Self-described realist review combining systematic database/grey-literature searching (8 databases + policy/government portals), explicit eligibility criteria, a PRISMA selection flow diagram (Figure 1, rendered as an image on p. 605), JBI + culturally adapted CREATE appraisal (Appendix A), and Indigenous collaborative 'yarning circles' with a Co-design Brains Trust. Two critical methodological caveats apply for Task I overlap and eligibility auditing: (1) Borderline Narrow Criterion 2 fit: Although the review defines policy as mandatory compliance with consequences, includes linkage to accountability mechanisms (e.g., regulation) as an inclusion criterion, and analyzes the non-enforceable legal status of the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines (ADWG) and lack of statutory human-right-to-water obligations across federal/state/local law, its primary research questions examine participatory co-design and integration of Indigenous knowledge in policy formulation rather than empirically testing legal, regulatory, tenure, or tariff rules governing last-mile WASH access. (2) Near-absence of primary empirical WASH studies among the 38 included sources: Table 1 lists 5 'peer-reviewed studies' and 33 grey literature files (24 government policy/strategy documents, 4 WSAA local case study vignettes, and 5 media releases/articles). Even within the 5 'peer-reviewed studies', only Wyrwoll et al. (2022) is an empirical water-quality/policy dataset analysis; Balasooriya et al. (2023) is itself a secondary literature review, Howey & Grealy (2021) is a legal/policy analysis appraised as expert opinion, Vanweydeveld & WSAA (2022) is an industry review report (not a peer-reviewed journal article, and also the apparent source of Case Study #1), and Moggridge & Thompson (2021) is an Indigenous perspective article (whose numbered superscript 42 in Table 1 was omitted from the alphabetical reference list). AMSTAR 2 is only borderline-fit for realist policy reviews and rates Critically Low due to lack of a registered protocol (Q2), no excluded-studies list (Q7), non-standard RoB assessment omitted entirely for 33/38 sources (Q9), and failure to incorporate appraisal flaws into result interpretation (Q13).
